newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar hovers under 119 yen after volatile day.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hovers under 119 yen after volatile day.

text.p: The dollar was clinging below 119 yen by late Tokyo on Monday, buffeted by comments from Japanese officials as operators waited warily for the start of European trading time.
Earlier in the day, the greenback had plunged to a nearly four-month low of 117.50 yen but managed to claw higher after a raft of supportive comments by Japanese officials.

The fragile greenback had even managed to climb back above 119 yen by mid-afternoon after short-covering emerged on the back of comments from Taku Yamasaki, chairman of the policy research council of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).
Yamasaki said that changing Japan's record-low interest rates would undermine the economy, adding that a level of around 120 yen to the dollar was most appropriate.

But the dollar's gains were undermined by late afternoon comments from Shoichiro Toyoda, chairman of powerful Japanese business lobby Keidanren, that current low Japanese interest rate levels will not continue.
Toyoda also said that a dollar rate of 110 to 120 yen reflects Japanese economic fundamentals, and that the Japanese economy is becoming firmer.

A city bank dealer said some profit-taking from operators who had bought the dollar at lower levels today had emerged. Some exporter offers were likely at this level, but another dealer said exporters were more likely to sell from 120 yen up.

Buying from importers continued to provide the dollar with support, although some dealers said this seemed to be tapering off a bit as many in the market feel the greenback still has room to fall further.

Some bids were also detected from Japanese life insurers, dealers said. Although many in the market had voiced concern that insurers could join with trust banks and securities firms, which have recently been dumping dollars to hedge their foreign assets, some insurers in fact seem to be seizing the chance to buy the greenback at bargain levels.

But dealers remained wary about overseas moves today. "The Asian market appears satisfied with today's low, but we may see another test of it overseas," said Akira Kurihara, a manager at the Norinchukin Bank, who added that the dollar could slip as low as 115 yen this week.
The credit-bank dealer said the technical picture was also dark. "If you look at the charts, there are still more selling than buying factors. It's too early to say falls are over."

But other dealers said such worries may be exaggerated, at least where today's overseas trade is concerned. "Today's comments by Japanese officials, and the fact that overseas markets already had a chance to sell on Friday, mean overseas operators are not as likely to engage in the type of panic sales we saw in Asia today," the city bank dealer said.
Senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said today that the dollar is likely to stabilise soon.

He was joined by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who said the dollar is likely to settle down soon as the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations' statement on foreign exchange rates is digested by foreign exchange markets.

The dollar also slid against the mark during Asian trade, at one point falling as low as 1.6680 marks before recovering. But dealers said these moves were mainly peripheral, with the dollar's fall against the yen dragging it down on the mark.
Singapore dealers agreed that the dollar looked vulnerable to further weakness during European trade. -- Singapore newsroom +65-8703080, Elaine Lies in Tokyo +81-3-3432-8806
